extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Cartesian philosophy; philosophers and general readers interested in epistemology and method
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Descartes' prescriptive epistemic and methodological principles from the Discourse on Method and the Meditations — rules for enquiry, standards of truth, and practical maxims for conducting inquiry. Useful for understanding criteria Descartes offers for establishing certain knowledge and for provisional conduct while seeking truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 1 — Accept only what is clear and distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Never accept anything as true unless it is presented so clearly and distinctly to the mind that there is no ground for doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundational methodological precept in the Discourse: avoid precipitous assent, withhold belief from any idea that is not evident. Descartes applies it as the first rule of his method for reaching certain knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 2 — Divide difficulties into simplest parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide each difficulty into as many parts as possible and necessary to resolve it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic decomposition: break complex problems into manageable components (modeled on mathematical problem-solving) so each can be understood clearly before synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 3 — Conduct thoughts from simple to complex
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct your thoughts in an orderly fashion, beginning with the simplest and most easily known objects and progressively ascending to the more complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synthetic reconstruction: once simple elements are established, combine them stepwise to build secure knowledge of more complex matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 4 — Make complete enumerations and thorough reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Make enumerations so complete, and reviews so general, that nothing is omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure completeness by systematic checking and review so that conclusions rest on exhaustive consideration rather than accidental omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodic doubt (systematic skepticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematically doubt any belief that can be called into question — including sensory judgments, beliefs grounded in habit, and even mathematical certainties — until reaching beliefs that resist doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descartes employs hyperbolic doubt (possibility of illusion, dreaming, and an all-deceiving evil demon) as a methodological tool to strip away uncertain beliefs and locate indubitable foundations for knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of the cogito (first indubitable truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposition 'I think, therefore I am' (cogito) is immediately certain: the very act of doubting/thinking demonstrates the existence of the thinking subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the first secure starting-point for rebuilding knowledge: existence of the self as a thinking thing is indubitable because thought presupposes a thinker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and distinct perception as criterion of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas that are perceived clearly (present and evident to attentive mind) and distinctly (precise and different from others) are to be judged true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descartes elevates clear-and-distinct perceptions to epistemic status, but he also discusses the need for a further warrant (God's veracity) to guarantee that what one perceives clearly and distinctly is not systematically deceptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: God's non-deceptive guarantee for truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The assurance that clear and distinct perceptions are reliable rests on the existence of a benevolent, non-deceiving God who is the cause of our clear ideas and would not permit universal deception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descartes offers arguments for God's existence (causal and ontological moves in the Meditations) to secure epistemic certainty: the divine guarantee bridges the gap between mental clarity and objective truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senses are fallible and not primary guarantors of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensory perceptions can deceive (illusions, dreams), so they cannot be trusted as ultimate foundations for knowledge unless corroborated by clear and distinct reason and the assurance of God's veracity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sensory data cautiously; derive certainty from reasoned, clear-and-distinct ideas rather than unexamined sense-impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind–body distinction (criterion of distinctness for substances)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind (a thinking, non-extended substance) and the body (an extended, non-thinking substance) are distinct because each can be clearly and distinctly conceived apart from the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descartes uses conceivability and clear distinctness as the test for distinct substances: if one can clearly and distinctly conceive X without Y, then X can exist independently of Y (supporting substance dualism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mathematical method (analysis and synthesis) in natural philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Emulate the rigor of mathematics: employ analytic decomposition to identify simple principles and synthetic construction to deduce complex truths; aim for certainty and clarity similar to geometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descartes recommends applying the mathematical method to other sciences — seeking first principles and building knowledge with the same logical rigor rather than relying on unexamined scholastic authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional moral rules while seeking truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a temporary practical code (obey laws and customs of one's country, be resolute in action, master oneself rather than fortune, and remain consistent) to govern conduct while one suspends judgement and pursues philosophical inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because radical doubt requires withholding many ordinary judgments, Descartes prescribes pragmatic maxims to live by (a provisional morality) so inquiry can proceed without moral or social disorder.
